slides.title: AST 102: Measuring the Stars
body_text: Distance, brightness, temperature
Dr. Alex Morgan
slides.speaker_notes: Welcome to AST 102. We start with the hardest question in astronomy: how far?

slides.title: How Far?
body_text: Every star is a point of light
A faint star could be dim and close or brilliant and far
We need a distance before anything else makes sense
slides.speaker_notes: Recap from AST 101: arcseconds and the inverse-square law.

slides.title: Parallax
body_text: The apparent shift of a nearby object against distant ones
Baseline: Earth's orbit, observations six months apart
Parallax angle p: half the total shift
Nearer stars have bigger parallax
slides.speaker_notes: Thumb blink demonstration. Hold the thumb closer and it jumps more.

slides.title: Parsecs
body_text: d = 1 / p, with d in parsecs and p in arcseconds
1 parsec = about 3.26 light-years
1 parsec = about 206,000 times the Earth-Sun distance
slides.speaker_notes: Parsec: parallax of one arcsecond. A unit built to make the formula a single division.

slides.title: The Nearest Stars
body_text: Proxima Centauri: p = 0.77 arcseconds, d = about 1.3 pc (4.2 light-years)
Sirius: p = 0.38 arcseconds, d = about 2.6 pc (8.6 light-years)
No star has a parallax as large as 1 arcsecond
slides.speaker_notes: Everyone gets 1.3 parsecs. Then ask: why is it more than 1? Because p is less than 1.

slides.title: The Limits of Parallax
body_text: At 100 pc, p = 0.01 arcseconds
Air turbulence blurs ground-based images by about 1 arcsecond
Space telescopes measure parallaxes to tens of millionths of an arcsecond
That reaches thousands of parsecs, a small part of the galaxy
slides.speaker_notes: Parallax is the first rung of the distance ladder. Everything farther is calibrated on it.

slides.title: The Magnitude Scale
body_text: Smaller magnitude = brighter star
5 magnitudes = a factor of exactly 100 in brightness
1 magnitude = a factor of about 2.512
Very bright objects have negative magnitudes: Sirius -1.5, the Sun -26.7
slides.speaker_notes: Golf scores: lower is better. The ancient catalogs called the brightest stars first magnitude.

slides.title: Absolute Magnitude
body_text: Apparent magnitude: how bright a star looks from Earth
Absolute magnitude: how bright it would look from 10 parsecs
The Sun's absolute magnitude is about 4.8
slides.speaker_notes: Absolute magnitude puts every star at the same distance so we can compare their real output.

slides.title: Stellar Colors
body_text: Hot stars look blue-white; cool stars look orange-red
Color measures surface temperature
In Orion: Betelgeuse is orange-red, Rigel is blue-white
slides.speaker_notes: Red is cool here. Faucets have it backwards for astronomy.

slides.title: Spectral Classes
body_text: O B A F G K M, from hottest to coolest
O stars: 30,000 K and up, blue; M stars: about 3,000 K, red
The Sun is a G2 star, about 5,800 K
Each class has subclasses 0 to 9
slides.speaker_notes: Students write their own mnemonic. The class votes on the best one.
